```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Find the repository from either the repository root or the analysis folder.
# Rendering rebuilds the supplement from the original aggregated CSV. It does
# not install packages, change the raw data, or contact any remote service.
roots <- c(".", "..")
roots <- roots[file.exists(file.path(roots, "scripts/07_peer_comparison_review.R"))]
if (!length(roots)) stop("Render inside the complete project repository.")
ROOT <- normalizePath(roots[1])
options(warn = 2, knitr.kable.NA = "Unknown")
source(file.path(ROOT, "scripts/07_peer_comparison_review.R"), local = TRUE)
review <- run_peer_review(ROOT, make_figures = TRUE)
tables <- review$tables
recent <- tables$peer_comparisons[tables$peer_comparisons$start_year == 2022, ]
before <- tables$peer_comparisons[tables$peer_comparisons$start_year == 2017, ]
number <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%+.1f%%", x)
pp <- function(x) sprintf("%+.1f pp", x)
show_table <- function(x, ...) knitr::kable(x, row.names = FALSE, ...)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = TRUE,
  error = FALSE, out.width = "100%")
```

# 1. What this adds to the report

The five cases all lost SME establishments between 2022 and 2024. The next
question is whether the same industries also lost establishments elsewhere.
That distinction changes the reason for selecting each case for closer review.

Three groups declined while their industry peers grew: **CBD professional
services, CBD construction and Southbank hospitality**. CBD finance and
administrative services also declined, but less sharply than their peers.
Their importance comes from the size of their remaining historical gaps.

The comparisons describe differences in business presence. They do not measure
the effect of COVID or predict the effect of a support programme.

# 2. Data and comparison method

We use the supplied CLUE file
`business-establishments-and-jobs-data-by-business-size-and-anzsic.csv`.
Small and Medium business categories are summed within each census year,
precinct and ANZSIC division. These categories cover establishments with
1–199 jobs. Missing job counts do not affect the establishment totals.

For each case, its reference is the **same industry in all other precincts**.
The focal precinct is excluded so it cannot influence its own benchmark.
We pool the counts before calculating growth: a precinct with one business
does not receive the same weight as one with hundreds.

```{r method-example}
# An example using the CBD professional-services case, 2022 to 2024.
# These quantities are rebuilt from the raw source by run_peer_review().
example <- recent[recent$case_rank == 1, ]
peer_growth <- example$peer_end / example$peer_start - 1
benchmark_count <- example$n_start * (1 + peer_growth)
observed_minus_benchmark <- example$n_end - benchmark_count
```

The CBD had `r number(example$n_start)` professional-services SMEs in 2022.
Applying the `r pct(100 * peer_growth)` growth of professional services
outside the CBD gives a comparison count of about `r number(benchmark_count)`
in 2024. The observed count was `r number(example$n_end)`, about
`r number(abs(observed_minus_benchmark))` below that reference.
The reference is a descriptive calculation, not a forecast or an estimate of
businesses lost because of a particular policy or event.

Comparisons use years at least two years apart. An absent precinct–industry–year
cell stays unknown. Published peer totals are accompanied by a matched-peer
check using only precincts observed in both years.

# 3. Recent change: three distinct local gaps

```{r recent-figure, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(ROOT,
  "outputs/figures/final/deeper_review/recent_peer_comparison.png"))
```

```{r recent-table, echo=FALSE}
display <- data.frame(
  Group = recent$label,
  `Local growth` = pct(recent$local_growth_pct),
  `Peer growth` = pct(recent$peer_growth_pct),
  `Difference` = pp(recent$growth_gap_pp),
  `Observed minus benchmark` = sprintf("%+.1f", recent$observed_minus_benchmark),
  check.names = FALSE)
show_table(display)
```

The professional-services gap combines a large existing sector with recent
underperformance. Construction has the widest percentage-point difference,
but starts from a smaller count. Southbank hospitality moves in the opposite
direction to hospitality elsewhere. Finance and administrative services need
a different explanation: their decline is shared across precincts, and the
CBD performed relatively better during this recent period.

The five cases together remain `r number(review$summary$selected_case_shortfall_2019)`
SMEs below their 2019 counts. Their `r number(abs(review$summary$selected_case_recent_change))`
net loss since 2022 is part of that historical gap; the two numbers must not
be added together.

# 4. Was relative weakness already present before 2020?

```{r pre-recent-figure, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(ROOT,
  "outputs/figures/final/deeper_review/pre_recent_comparison.png"))
```

CBD professional services grew more slowly than peers in both 2017–2019
(`r pp(before$growth_gap_pp[1])`) and 2022–2024 (`r pp(recent$growth_gap_pp[1])`).
This recent gap is not entirely new. Construction and Southbank hospitality
were ahead of peers in the earlier window and behind them in the recent one.

Earlier windows give a mixed picture. Professional services underperformed in
only three of eight non-overlapping pre-period comparisons from 2003–2005 to
2017–2019, and outperformed peers in 2020–2022. The alternate even-year
pre-period scheme gives five of eight underperformances. We therefore describe
weakness in the two selected windows without claiming an uninterrupted
historical trend or a permanent structural break.

```{r history-figure, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(ROOT,
  "outputs/figures/final/deeper_review/full_two_year_history.png"))
```

# 5. How much do the cases depend on our choices?

## Recent-decline cutoff

The four scale cases are the largest 2019–2024 shortfalls among groups that
also declined by at least 2% in 2022–2024. The fifth case is selected separately:
the largest hospitality shortfall outside the CBD among continuing declines.

The same four scale cases appear with a 1%, 2% or 3% recent-decline cutoff.
At 0%, CBD health care replaces construction. At 5%, only two of the four
original scale cases remain. The 2% cutoff is a practical case-selection
choice, not a test of statistical significance.

```{r threshold-table, echo=FALSE}
s <- tables$threshold_stability
s <- s[s$baseline_year == 2019, ]
show_table(data.frame(
  `Recent decline cutoff` = paste0(s$threshold_pct, "%"),
  `Original four retained` = paste0(s$original_scale_cases_retained, "/4"),
  `Same four cases` = ifelse(s$same_scale_set_as_2019_two_percent, "Yes", "No"),
  check.names = FALSE))
```

## Baseline year

Using 2018 changes the shortlist. North Melbourne professional services
replaces CBD construction, and Docklands replaces Southbank as the hospitality
contrast. The first three CBD cases remain. All original five still have
fewer SMEs in 2024 than in either baseline year, but their ranking and gap sizes
depend on that choice.

```{r baseline-table, echo=FALSE}
b <- tables$baseline_sensitivity
b18 <- b[b$baseline_year == 2018, ]
b19 <- b[b$baseline_year == 2019, ]
show_table(data.frame(Group = b18$label,
  `2018 count` = b18$n_baseline, `2019 count` = b19$n_baseline,
  `2024 count` = b18$n_2024,
  `Change from 2018` = pct(b18$baseline_change_pct),
  `Change from 2019` = pct(b19$baseline_change_pct), check.names = FALSE))
```

This matters most for Southbank hospitality: 2024 is just 1.9% below 2018,
compared with 14.4% below 2019. Its recent underperformance remains, but the
size of its historical shortfall should be tied explicitly to the 2019 baseline.
The complete alternative roster is exported in `baseline_case_selection.csv`.

## Peer composition

Excluding the CBD as well as Southbank still leaves hospitality peers growing
by `r pct(tables$hospitality_reference_sensitivity$peer_growth_pct[2])`, compared
with Southbank's `r pct(recent$local_growth_pct[5])`. The local divergence is
not explained solely by a strong CBD rebound.

Construction has one establishment in a newly observed peer cell in 2024.
Using only peer precincts observed in both years reduces peer growth from
13.9% to 13.3%. It does not change the conclusion. Every exported comparison
includes peer coverage and matched-peer growth so this can be checked directly.

# 6. What this means for the report

Use the peer comparison to explain **why** each case is important. Professional
services, construction and Southbank hospitality show local underperformance
against growing peers. Finance and administrative services show large
remaining gaps within industries that also declined elsewhere.

This supports differentiated priorities for further investigation. It does
not establish the causes of the gaps, identify individual business closures,
or show which intervention would work. Those claims need additional evidence.

# 7. Reproducibility

The supplement is built by `scripts/07_peer_comparison_review.R`; it can also
be sourced and run as `run_peer_review(root, make_figures = TRUE)`. Tables and
figures are written under `outputs/*/final/deeper_review/`. The source checksum
and R session details are saved alongside them. The raw file is unchanged.

`tests/test_peer_comparison_review.R` independently recomputes comparisons,
rankings and history from the raw CSV, and checks missing-cell behaviour,
zero denominators and the two-year comparison rule. Run it with:

```{r test-command, eval=FALSE}
# From the repository root, in a terminal:
# Rscript tests/test_peer_comparison_review.R
```

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
